name: Androgen deficiency in the ageing male (late-onset hypogonadism)

reference.source: Campbell-Walsh-Wein Urology / WHO laboratory manual for semen analysis
clinicalPearls: The diagnosis rests on the combination of persistent, characteristic symptoms together with unequivocally low serum testosterone; neither a low level alone nor symptoms alone is sufficient
Sexual features are the most specific complaints and include reduced libido, poorer spontaneous morning erections, and erectile difficulty, alongside fatigue, reduced muscle bulk, and depressed mood
Testosterone should be sampled in the early morning when concentrations peak and any low result confirmed on a second fasting specimen before labelling a man deficient
Calculated free or bioavailable testosterone is more informative when sex-hormone-binding globulin is altered, as occurs with ageing, obesity, and systemic illness
Addressing reversible contributors such as obesity, poorly controlled diabetes, and the metabolic syndrome can meaningfully raise endogenous testosterone and should precede replacement in many men
Before and during testosterone replacement, haematocrit, prostate-specific antigen, and a prostate examination should be checked because therapy can provoke erythrocytosis and unmask prostate disease
Replacement is contraindicated in untreated prostate or breast cancer, and caution applies with polycythaemia, untreated severe obstructive sleep apnoea, and unstable cardiac disease
Exogenous testosterone suppresses spermatogenesis, so men wishing to preserve fertility should instead be considered for gonadotropin-based treatment
reference.pathophysiology: Serum testosterone declines gradually with advancing age through combined defects at several levels of the hypothalamic-pituitary-testicular axis. There is a reduction in Leydig cell number and secretory capacity (a primary testicular component) alongside blunting of luteinising hormone pulse amplitude and altered hypothalamic drive (a secondary central component), so gonadotropins are often only modestly elevated. A progressive rise in sex-hormone-binding globulin further lowers the free fraction available to tissues. Comorbidities that accumulate with age, particularly obesity, type 2 diabetes, the metabolic syndrome, and chronic illness, suppress the axis and amplify the fall, meaning much of the observed deficiency is functional rather than fixed organic gonadal failure.
additionalDifferentials: Classical organic hypogonadism such as Klinefelter syndrome or prior testicular injury
Pituitary or hypothalamic pathology including prolactinoma and other sellar tumours
Depression and other primary mood disorders
Anaemia or chronic systemic illness producing fatigue
Drug effects, particularly opioids, glucocorticoids, and antiandrogens
additionalInvestigations: Early-morning fasting total testosterone, repeated on a second occasion to confirm a low result
Sex-hormone-binding globulin with calculated free or bioavailable testosterone when binding protein is abnormal
Luteinising hormone and follicle-stimulating hormone to distinguish primary from secondary hypogonadism
Serum prolactin, with pituitary imaging if a central cause or markedly low gonadotropins are found
Iron studies and ferritin to screen for haemochromatosis in suspected primary failure
Baseline haematocrit and prostate-specific antigen prior to any replacement
Metabolic assessment including HbA1c and lipid profile given the strong association with cardiometabolic disease
redFlags: Visual field loss, persistent headache, or other features suggesting a pituitary mass
Very low testosterone with inappropriately low or normal gonadotropins pointing to central pathology
A breast mass or gynaecomastia raising concern for oestrogen excess or malignancy
A rising prostate-specific antigen or abnormal prostate on examination
Marked erythrocytosis developing on replacement therapy
reference.prognosis: In men with genuine symptomatic deficiency confirmed biochemically, replacement typically improves libido, mood, energy, and body composition, while lifestyle and comorbidity optimisation can restore endogenous production in functional cases; long-term outcomes depend on careful monitoring for prostate and haematological effects and on treating the underlying cardiometabolic burden.
pitfalls: Diagnosing deficiency from a single random or afternoon sample rather than a confirmed early-morning value
Commencing replacement in men with borderline levels and few or non-specific symptoms
Overlooking a treatable secondary cause such as hyperprolactinaemia or a pituitary tumour
Failing to monitor haematocrit and prostate-specific antigen during therapy
Prescribing testosterone to a man who wishes to father children, thereby suppressing his sperm production
references: European Association of Urology guidelines on sexual and reproductive health
WHO laboratory manual for the examination and processing of human semen
management: Optimise reversible functional contributors first — weight reduction, glycaemic control in type 2 diabetes and treatment of the metabolic syndrome, which can restore endogenous testosterone before any replacement
Testosterone replacement, by transdermal gel or intramuscular ester, in men with persistent characteristic symptoms and biochemically confirmed low early-morning testosterone
Treat associated erectile dysfunction with phosphodiesterase-5 inhibitors alongside hormonal correction
Preserve fertility with gonadotropin therapy rather than exogenous testosterone in men still seeking fatherhood, since replacement suppresses spermatogenesis
Monitor haematocrit for therapy-induced erythrocytosis, managing with dose reduction or venesection if it develops
Baseline and periodic prostate-specific antigen with prostate examination to detect unmasked prostate disease during replacement
Avoid testosterone in untreated prostate or breast cancer and in decompensated heart failure, and assess bone density given fracture risk
